p.x:
Last weekend, my family went to Doi Inthanon, the highest mountain in Thailand. We got up at 4 a.m. to see the sunrise from the top. It was very cold, but the view was amazing!
After breakfast, we walked along a path through the forest. My dad carried a big backpack with water and food. We stopped at a beautiful waterfall and took lots of photos.
In the afternoon, we visited a small cave. It was dark inside, so we used torches. On the way back, we saw a helicopter flying over the mountains. My little brother wanted to climb a tree with a rope, but my mum said no!

Northern Thailand is a great place for trekking. Many visitors go on a two- or three-day trek through the mountains, staying in hill tribe villages at night.
The scenery is beautiful: green valleys, rice fields and misty peaks. Most trails are easy, but some parts are very steep, especially when the slope is wet and muddy. Good shoes are essential, and you'll need a warm sleeping bag because nights can be surprisingly cold.
Always go with a local guide. The forest can be confusing, and some paths pass close to the edge of a cliff. Guides know the safest routes and can tell you about the plants and animals.
For more serious climbers, the Himalayas are the next step. There, a mountaineer must deal with high altitude, extreme cold and the danger of an avalanche or blizzard. Expeditions usually start from a base camp, and local porters help carry equipment. Climbers wear a harness and use ropes on narrow ridges. Above the clouds, they may cross a huge glacier. Many say the descent is harder than the climb, because they are so tired. Reaching the summit is a dream for many, but it requires months of preparation.

Every year, thousands of people attempt to climb the world's highest mountains. For some, it is the ultimate test of endurance; for others, a spiritual journey. Whatever the motivation, high-altitude mountaineering remains one of the most dangerous activities on Earth.
The greatest risk comes from the environment itself. Above 8,000 metres, in what climbers call the 'death zone', the air contains so little oxygen that the human body begins to deteriorate. Climbers must acclimatise slowly, spending weeks moving up and down the mountain so that their bodies can adjust. Even so, they face frostbite, which can destroy fingers and toes, and hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature. The rugged terrain adds further danger: ice can make paths treacherous, and a single slip can be fatal.
The success of many expeditions depends on the Sherpa people of Nepal, whose knowledge of the mountains and remarkable ability to work at altitude are essential. Living in villages in the foothills of the Himalayas, many Sherpas have guided foreign climbers for generations, often taking the greatest risks for relatively little reward.
In recent years, critics have raised concerns about overcrowding on popular peaks, where queues of climbers wait for hours during the final ascent. Some argue that the desire to conquer a mountain has become a form of tourism rather than adventure. For most people, though, the mountains offer simpler pleasures: fresh air, open views and, for those who suffer from vertigo, a healthy respect for keeping both feet on the ground.
